html:
In 1848 France's new Second Republic gave the people of its oldest towns in Senegal the rights of French citizens, including the vote. These towns, Saint-Louis, Gorée, Rufisque and Dakar, became known as the Four Communes.

The same revolution of 1848 ended slavery in the French colonies. Saint-Louis and Gorée had been French trading posts for centuries, with mixed African and French families. Rufisque and Dakar were added in the 1880s. Their African-born residents, the originaires, could elect a deputy to the National Assembly in Paris. Elsewhere in French West Africa Africans were subjects with no such rights.

French officials kept trying to narrow these rights. In 1914 the voters elected Blaise Diagne, the first black African deputy in the French parliament. During the First World War he won a law in 1916 confirming the citizenship of the originaires, in return for helping recruit West African soldiers for France.

The Communes gave Senegal a long tradition of elections and politics. Léopold Sédar Senghor later rose through this system.
